Commentary.Commentary: Back with the chase! The players of Sri Lanka are out there, dispersing to take their respective positions, while the two openers of Pakistan stride out as well. Sahibzada Farhan will open the innings alongside Fakhar Zaman. Nuwan Thushara will start the proceedings. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right then, 134 is what stands between Pakistan and the crucial two points. The pitch has grip, but not unplayable demons, and with dew potentially aiding batting later, the Pakistani openers will fancy making the most of the Powerplay. Sri Lanka’s only hope lies in early wickets with the new ball, or else Pakistan might stroll home in this crunch game. The chase is in a bit, so hop on!

From there, it was always going to be a rescue act. Wanindu Hasaranga was dismissed by Abrar Ahmed, who was absolutely BRILLIANT with his spell of 4-0-8-1, choking the middle overs. Kamindu Mendis, however, stood tall under pressure with a fighting 50 and stitched a small stand with Chamika Karunaratne. Together they eked out some runs, but Pakistan’s discipline with the ball never let the Lankans break free. Shaheen ended with 3/28, while Haris Rauf picked two, ensuring the target stayed within Pakistan’s reach.

The skipper, Salman Agha, won the toss and invited Sri Lanka to bat first. It all began with Shaheen Afridi breathing fire with the new ball, dismissing Kusal Mendis for a duck on just the second delivery and then Pathum Nissanka soon after, reducing Sri Lanka to 18/2. Kusal Perera’s brief counter was cut short by Haris Rauf after a STUNNING catch from Faheem Ashraf, leaving the Lankans rattled at 43/3 inside the Powerplay. Skipper Charith Asalanka tried to steady things, but Hussain Talat’s twin strikes in back-to-back balls, including Asalanka and the dangerous in-form Shanaka, left them reeling at 58/5.

Is this enough? A total of 133? On a big night in Abu Dhabi, it certainly doesn’t feel like, as Sri Lanka have stumbled to a MODEST score in this crucial Super Four clash. Pakistan, who came in under pressure after their last defeat, have bowled with fire and precision. The last few overs saw Kamindu Mendis complete a fighting half-century before Shaheen Afridi struck again, and despite his resistance, the Lankans could not stretch beyond 133/8. Who has the edge? Surely, Pakistan do.

A couple of runs to end the innings! Rauf sticks to the pace off option and this is on a good length, on off. Chamika Karunaratne waits deep in the crease but does not quite get hold of it as he hoicks across the line. Gets it to the right of deep mid-wicket. There is a slight misfield in the deep and Chamika is keen for the third run but Maheesh isn't. A brace on the final ball results in Sri Lanka ending with 133 on the board!

Now, Sri Lanka need to build a partnership to reach a respectable total, while Pakistan will be aiming to kill the game as quickly as possible with the ball by taking more wickets. SIX! All the way! Haris Rauf bangs it into the deck but he fails to get it high enough. It is around the waist and the pace is 134.6 kph. Kamindu climbs into it as he swivels and pulls it towards deep backward square leg. The fielder in the deep just watches the ball sail over his head. End of an eventful Powerplay. Sri Lanka are 53/3.
Commentary.Default_Commentary: 5.6: Haris Rauf to Kamindu Mendis, Six!

Commentary.Commentary: FOUR! Lovely shot and Kamindu Mendis is up and running! On a good length, fractionally wide on off. Kamindu lets the ball come to him and just taps the ball on its head. Caresses it through cover-point for his first runs.
Commentary.Default_Commentary: 5.5: Haris Rauf to Kamindu Mendis, Four!

Commentary.Commentary: The national anthems are done, and the two umpires now make their way out to the centre. It is a decent turnout tonight at the Zayed Cricket Stadium. No matter the numbers, the supporters of the two teams will surely make their presence felt. Salman Agha and Co. disperse from the huddle, and they are followed by the two Sri Lankan openers, Pathum Nissanka and Kusal Mendis. Shaheen Afridi has the new ball in hand. Shaheen to Nissanka first up. A slip in place. Let's play...

We are just moments away from the start of the game. Charith Asalanka and Salman Agha lead their respective teams out for the national anthems. It will be Sri Lanka's national anthem first, followed by that of Pakistan.

PITCH REPORT - Urooj Mumtaz is near the deck. She starts by providing some numbers, with 170 being the average 1st innings score at this ground and 183 being the average 1st innings winning score. Simon Doull joins her, and he says that this is a fantastic wicket with a good covering of grass. Believes that the grass covering will aid in the ball coming onto the bat nicely. Opines that there will be some movement upfront with the new ball, but there won't be much turn on offer for the spinners. Urooj points out that pacers have been more successful at this venue than the spinners. Doull suggests that the pacers should look to bowl the Test match lengths while the batters should make use of the slight breeze, which is blowing across the ground. He reckons that Sri Lanka should look to score around 180-190 to be ahead in the game.

Pakistan (Unchanged Playing XI) - Sahibzada Farhan, Fakhar Zaman, Saim Ayub, Hussain Talat, Mohammad Nawaz, Salman Agha (C), Faheem Ashraf, Mohammad Haris (WK), Shaheen Afridi, Haris Rauf, and Abrar Ahmed.

Sri Lanka (Playing XI) - Pathum Nissanka, Kusal Mendis (WK), Kusal Perera, Dasun Shanaka, Charith Asalanka (C), Kamindu Mendis, Chamika Karunaratne (In place of Kamil Mishara), Wanindu Hasaranga, Maheesh Theekshana (In place of Dunith Wellalage), Dushmantha Chameera, and Nuwan Thushara.

Sri Lanka's skipper, Charith Asalanka, says that he would have also preferred to bowl first, but is fine with batting first now. Feels that the side has been playing good cricket, though there are still areas to improve, especially death bowling. Informs two changes to the XI, with Maheesh Theekshana and Chamika Karunaratne coming in. On the team balance, he adds that they felt the need for one extra bowler who can also contribute with the bat.

The captain of Pakistan, Salman Agha, feels that this is a good wicket and believes that the surface won't change much. Mentions that they started well against India but lost their way between overs 10 to 15. Adds that they want to start well with the ball in this game. Shares that they are not worried about how they have fared against Sri Lanka in the past and they are looking forward to this new challenge. Informs that they are unchanged for this game.
TOSS - The flip of the coin lands in favour of Pakistan, and their skipper, Salman Agha, has elected to FIELD first.

The surface in Abu Dhabi has usually been friendlier for batters than Dubai, but it still gives slower bowlers something to work with. Conditions could bring spin into play as the game progresses, and chasing has not been straightforward here. It’s Pakistan’s firepower against Sri Lanka’s balance, both desperate to bounce back. With all that to keep, stick around for the toss and team lineups!

Key battles to watch? Haris Rauf vs Pathum Nissanka in the Powerplay, as Rauf has 5 wickets in just 2 T20Is against Sri Lanka. Shaheen Afridi vs Kusal Mendis. Can Pakistan’s left-arm spearhead finally strike early? And don’t miss Nuwan Thushara’s battle against Sahibzada Farhan, who is Pakistan’s in-form batter. These mini-duels could well decide the edge in today's game.

Problems of Sri Lanka? Their issue is consistency under pressure. Pathum Nissanka and Kusal Mendis gave them a solid start against Bangladesh, while Dasun Shanaka’s unbeaten 64 was a good knock. But the middle order still hasn’t shown the resilience required in tight contests. With the ball, Wanindu Hasaranga remains a proven match-winner, taking 2/22 in the last game, but he lacked support. Nuwan Thushara leaked runs and must bounce back. Sri Lanka lean heavily on their top order and their spinners, as they need both departments clicking if they are to push for a spot in the final.

Need of Pakistan? First, stability in their batting. Sahibzada Farhan stood tall against India, but beyond him, no one truly anchored the innings until Faheem Ashraf’s late burst. Their total of 171 looked good, but wasn’t defended. Why? Because the bowling lacked sharpness. Shaheen Afridi went wicketless and expensive, and the spin duo, Abrar Ahmed and Saim Ayub, failed to control the middle overs. Haris Rauf was the only bright spot with 2/26. Pakistan’s challenge is clear - rediscover bite in the attack and get more than one batter firing at the top.

The Asia Cup Super Four stage is getting tighter, and Abu Dhabi is set for a crucial clash between Pakistan and Sri Lanka. What’s at stake? Two crucial points in the race to the final. Both sides are coming off losses in their first Super Four games, which makes this encounter almost a do-or-die battle. Pakistan were outplayed by India, while Sri Lanka stumbled against Bangladesh. Head-to-head? Pakistan lead overall 13-10, but Sri Lanka have won the last five meetings in this format. History, momentum, and survival are all on the line. On that note, hello and welcome to this big one from the Zayed Cricket Stadium.
... MATCH DAY ...

After a short breather of a day, the Asia Cup 2025 Super Four stage is back with Sri Lanka taking on Pakistan in a crunch clash at the Zayed Cricket Stadium. Both sides slipped in their opening Super Four games, where Sri Lanka lost a last-over close match to Bangladesh, while Pakistan were humbled by India. With only three games each in this stage, and India and Bangladesh already holding an early advantage, the stakes could not be higher. Which team can shrug off its scars and keep the final dream alive? Let’s know a bit about the Lions first. What’s going on with Sri Lanka? They had the firepower but lacked the finish in Dubai. Dasun Shanaka’s explosive 64 unbeaten off 37 gave them a strong 168/7, but the bowlers, barring Wanindu Hasaranga, couldn’t hold their nerve as Bangladesh chased with a ball to spare. Pathum Nissanka and Kusal Mendis have been steady run-getters in this tournament, while Shanaka’s cameo showed a fire under pressure. Yet, concerns remain - Kamil Mishara’s scratchy knock and Kamindu Mendis’s poor outing meant the middle order wobbled. On the bowling side, Nuwan Thushara and Dushmantha Chameera leaked runs, and Dunith Wellalage went wicketless. Is it time for Sri Lanka to recalibrate their bowling attack, or simply back their experienced names to deliver at the right time? What needs to click for the Lankans? Consistency in the Powerplay, both with bat and ball. With Pathum Nissanka in the top runs chart and Hasaranga delivering with 5 wickets at a miserly economy of under 6 so far, the pillars are there. But Thushara, despite 6 wickets in the tournament, has been expensive at over 7 economy, while Chameera’s high economy remains a concern in the death overs. The Lions must also find a way to turn their cameos into match-defining innings. Can Asalanka or Perera provide that missing stability? Or will Shanaka’s big hits be their lifeline again? Meanwhile, what about Pakistan? Their story is also familiar, from flashes of brilliance to being undone by inconsistency. Sahibzada Farhan looked elegant in his 58, and Faheem Ashraf’s late cameo gave them 171 against India. But the bowling, traditionally their strong suit, faltered. Shaheen Afridi went wicketless and expensive, Saim Ayub’s experimental overs bled over 11 per over, and only Haris Rauf looked threatening as he took two wickets. Batting has positives - Fakhar Zaman is finding touch, and Mohammad Nawaz’s 21 showed grit. Yet, over-reliance on one or two knocks has left them vulnerable. The big question - who will provide that complete team performance they so badly need? Where must Pakistan improve? With the ball in the middle overs. Abrar Ahmed and Haris Rauf are carrying the load, while Shaheen’s barren spells hurt the balance. With the bat, Farhan has been consistent at the top, but the middle order - Talat, Nawaz, Agha - must build partnerships instead of cameos. Pakistan also lack a power finisher, but can they do it against Sri Lanka’s spinners? So, what’s the buildup like? Abu Dhabi has offered scores around 170-plus in some games, challenging but chaseable. The pitch has grip for spinners, yet rewards clean hitting through the line. Sri Lanka’s spin could test Pakistan’s middle order, while Pakistan’s pace battery has the raw edge to unsettle Sri Lanka’s top order. Fans still remember the 2022 Asia Cup Final, when Sri Lanka stunned Pakistan the last time they met each other in this format. Could history repeat itself, or will Pakistan finally strike back? With both teams wounded and desperate, expect tension, tactical shifts, and possibly a nail-biter.
